'''Henbane''' ('''''Hyoscyamus niger''''', also '''black henbane''' and '''stinking nightshade''') is a poisonous plant belonging to tribe [[Hyoscyameae]] of the nightshade family [[Solanaceae]].<ref name="Kennedy 2014">{{cite book |last=Kennedy |first=David O. |year=2014 |chapter=The Deliriants: The Nightshade (''Solanaceae'') Family |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YUNDAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA131 |title=Plants and the Human Brain |location=[[New York City|New York]] |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |pages=131–7 |isbn=978-0-19-991401-2 |oclc=865508649 |lccn=2013031617}}</ref><ref name="Roberts_31">{{Harvnb|Wink|1998|p=31}}</ref> Henbane is native to [[Temperate climate|temperate]] [[Europe]] and [[Siberia]], and naturalised in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]].<ref>{{cite web |first1=T.D. |last1=Dines |first2=S.M. |last2=Smart |first3=K.J. |last3=Walker |title=Henbane ''Hyoscyamus niger'' L. |editor-first=P.A. |editor-last=Stroh |editor2-first=T.A. |editor2-last=Humphrey |editor3-first=R.J. |editor3-last=Burkmar |editor4-first=O.L. |editor4-last=Pescott |editor5-first=D.B. |editor5-last=Roy |editor6-first=K.J. |editor6-last=Walker |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fcr }}</ref>

==Historical use==
The name ''henbane'' dates from AD 1265; "bane" meant 'thing that causes death'.<ref>{{cite book | title = An Analytic Dictionary of English Etymology: An Introduction | first1 = Anatoly |last1=Liberman |first2=J. Lawrence |last2=Mitchell | publisher = University of Minnesota Press | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-8166-5272-3 | pages = 108–110 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_m7k1Oi-cakC&q=henbane+An+Analytic+Dictionary+of+English&pg=PA108 }}</ref> Other etymologies of ''henbane'' derive from the Indo-European stem ''bhelena'' meaning "crazy plant"<ref>{{Cite book|title=Bilsenkraut. Reallexikon der germanischen Altertumskunde|last=Hoops|first=J.|year=1973|pages=1:284}}</ref> and with the Proto-Germanic element ''bil'' meaning "vision", "hallucination", "magical power", and "miraculous ability".<ref>{{Cite book|chapter=Heilige Bäume, Bilsenkraut und Bildzeitung<!--Possibly originally all lower case, but WP practice is to normalise all that--> |last=de Vries|first=H.|location=Suedergellersen, Germany |publisher=Bruno Martin|year=1993 |title=Naturverehrung und Heilkunst |editor-first=C. |editor-last=Rätsch|pages=65–83}}</ref>

Historically, henbane was used in combination with other plants, such as the [[Mandragora officinarum|mandrake]], the [[deadly nightshade]], and [[datura]], as an anaesthetic potion, and for its psychoactive properties in "magic brews".<ref name="Kennedy 2014"/><ref name="Roberts_31" /><ref name="carter2003">{{cite journal | volume = 96 | date = March 2003 | journal = Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine | title = Myths and mandrakes | first = Anthony John |last=Carter | pages = 144–147 | pmc = 539425 | doi = 10.1177/014107680309600312 | pmid = 12612119 | issue = 3 }}</ref><ref name="carter1996">{{cite journal | journal = British Medical Journal | date = 1996 | volume = 313 | issue = 7072 | pages = 1630–1632 | pmc = 2359130 | title = Narcosis and nightshade | first = A. J. |last=Carter | pmid = 8991015| doi=10.1136/bmj.313.7072.1630}}</ref><ref name="Fatur 140–158">{{Cite journal|last=Fatur|first=Karsten|date=June 2020|title='Hexing Herbs' in Ethnobotanical Perspective: A Historical Review of the Uses of Anticholinergic Solanaceae Plants in Europe|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s12231-020-09498-w|journal=Economic Botany|language=en|volume=74|issue=2|pages=140–158|doi=10.1007/s12231-020-09498-w|bibcode=2020EcBot..74..140F |s2cid=220844064|issn=0013-0001|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  These psychoactive properties include visual hallucinations and a sensation of flight.<ref name="Schultes_22">Schultes & Smith 1976, p. 22</ref> It was originally used in [[continental Europe]], [[Asia]], and the [[Arab world]],<ref>{{cite book |first1=Joseph |last1=Perez |first2=Janet |last2=Lloyd |title=The Spanish Inquisition |publisher=Yale University Press |location= |date=2006 |isbn=978-0-300-11982-4 |pages=229 footnote 10 }}</ref> though it did spread to England in the [[Middle Ages]]. The use of henbane by the [[ancient Rome|ancient Romans]] was documented by [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]], who said it was "of the nature of wine and therefore offensive to the understanding", and by [[Dioscorides]], who recommended it as a sedative and [[analgesic]].<ref name="Grieve, Maud 1971">{{cite book |title=A Modern Herbal: The Medicinal, Culinary, Cosmetic and Economic Properties, Cultivation and Folk-lore of Herbs, Grasses, Fungi, Shrubs, & Trees with All Their Modern Scientific Uses |volume=1 |last=Grieve |first=Maud |year=1971}}</ref>

The plant, recorded as {{lang|la|Herba Apollinaris}}, was used to yield oracles by the priestesses of [[Apollo]].<ref name="Roberts_31" /> Recently evidence for its use in the earlier British Neolithic has been debated.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Deborah J. |last1=Long |first2=Paula |last2=Milburn |first3=M. Jane |last3=Bunting |first4=Richard |last4=Tipping |first5=Timothy G. |last5=Holden |title=Black Henbane (''Hyoscyamus niger'' L.) in the Scottish Neolithic: A Re-evaluation of Palynological Findings from Grooved Ware Pottery at Balfarg Riding School and Henge, Fife |journal=Journal of Archaeological Science |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=45–52 |date=January 1999 |doi=10.1006/jasc.1998.0308|bibcode=1999JArSc..26...45L }}</ref> [[John Gerard]]'s ''Herball'' states: "The leaves, the seeds and the juice, when taken internally cause an unquiet sleep, like unto the sleep of drunkenness, which continueth long and is deadly to the patient. To wash the feet in a decoction of Henbane, as also the often smelling of the flowers causeth sleep."<ref name="Grieve, Maud 1971"/>

The plant was also purportedly used as a fumigant for magical purposes.<ref name="Fatur 140–158"/> [[Albertus Magnus]], in his work {{lang|la|De Vegetalibus}} (1250), reported that [[necromancers]] used henbane to invoke the souls of the dead as well as demons.<ref name=Raetsch05>{{Cite book|title=The encyclopedia of psychoactive plants: ethnopharmacology and its applications|last=Rätsch|first=C.|publisher=Park Street Press|year=2005|pages=277–282}}</ref> Henbane was already being demonized as early as the [[Late Middle Ages]] when it became inseparably associated with witchcraft and [[Maleficium (sorcery)|malefic]] practices. "The witches drank the decoction of henbane and had those dreams for which they were tortured and executed. It was also used for witches' ointments and was used for making weather and conjuring spirits. If there were a great drought then a stalk of henbane would be dipped into a spring, then the sun-baked sand would be sprinkled with this" (Perger 1864, 181).<ref name=Raetsch05/>

Henbane was discovered among an assortment of imported spices during the underwater archaeological excavation of the royal Danish-Norwegian flagship, {{lang|da|[[Gribshunden]]}}, which sank in 1495 near Ronneby, Sweden. The purpose of this henbane is not known, but could have been medicinal for soothing toothache, or as an anti-emetic and to prevent motion sickness.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Larsson |first1=Mikael |last2=Foley |first2=Brendan |date=2023-01-26 |title=The king's spice cabinet–Plant remains from Gribshunden, a 15th century royal shipwreck in the Baltic Sea |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=18 |issue=1 |article-number=e0281010 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0281010 |doi-access=free |pmc=9879437 |pmid=36701280|bibcode=2023PLoSO..1881010L }}</ref>

During a [[Duchy of Pomerania|Pomeranian]] witchcraft trial in 1538, a suspected witch "confessed" that she had given a man henbane seeds so that he would run around "crazy" (sexually aroused). In a file from an Inquisition trial, it was noted that "a witch admits" having once strewn henbane seeds between two lovers and uttering the following formula: "Here I sow wild seed, and the devil advised that they would hate and avoid each other until these seeds had been separated" (Marzell 1922, 169).<ref name=Raetsch05/>

Henbane was one of the ingredients in [[gruit]], traditionally used in beers as a flavouring. The recipe for henbane beer includes 40 g dried chopped henbane herbage, 5 g bayberry, 23 L water, 1 L brewing malt, 900 g honey, 5 g dried yeast, and brown sugar.<ref name=Raetsch05/> Henbane fell out of usage for beer when it was replaced by [[hops]] in the 11th to 16th centuries; in Bavaria the [[Reinheitsgebot|Purity Law]] of 1516 outlawed ingredients other than barley, hops, yeast, and water.<ref>{{cite book | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=XRyxWu8rRnQC&q=grut+henbane&pg=PR12 | title = The Dictionary of Beer and Brewing | first1 = Dan |last1=Rabin |first2=Carl |last2=Forget | publisher = Taylor & Francis | year = 1998 | isbn = 978-1-57958-078-0 | no-pp = true | page = xii |chapter=Preface |chapter-url={{GBurl|XRyxWu8rRnQC|pg=PR12}} |quote=In approximately 768, Germans had first added hops to brew kettles.}}</ref>

Henbane is sometimes identified with the "[[hebenon]]" poured into the ear of [[Hamlet]]'s father,<ref name="carter2003" /><ref>{{cite dictionary |  title = Hebenon |  url = http://machaut.uchicago.edu/?action=search&word=hebenon&resource=Webster%27s&quicksearch=on | dictionary = Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913 + 1828) |  archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090724214156/http://machaut.uchicago.edu/?action=search&word=hebenon&resource=Webster%27s&quicksearch=on | archive-date = 2009-07-24 }}</ref> although other candidates for hebenon exist.<ref>{{cite book | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=_m7k1Oi-cakC&q=hebenon+henbane&pg=PA110 | title = An Analytic Dictionary of English Etymology: An Introduction |first1=Anatoly |last1=Liberman |first2=J. Lawrence |last2=Mitchell | publisher = University of Minnesota Press | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-8166-5272-3 | pages = 110–111 }}</ref>

=== Theories ===

Henbane seeds have been found in a [[Viking]] grave near [[Fyrkat]], Denmark, that was first described in 1977.<ref>{{Cite book|title= The Viking way: religion and war in late Iron Age Scandinavia |last=Price |first=Neil S.|date= 2002|publisher=Department of Archaeology and Ancient History, [[Uppsala University]] |isbn= 978-91-506-1626-2|location= Uppsala|oclc= 52987118}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Pentz|first1=Peter|last2=Baastrup Panum| first2= Maria| last3=Karg| first3= Sabine |last4= Mannering|first4=Ulla|date=2009|title=Kong Haralds vølve |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236874706|journal= Nationalmuseets Arbejdsmark | via= researchgate.net |pages=215–232|quote= Da graven og gravpladsen blev beskrevet første gang (1977) ... |trans-quote=When the grave and burial site were first described (1977) ...}}</ref> This and other archaeological finds show that ''H. niger'' was known to the Vikings. Analysis of the symptoms caused by intoxication of this plant suggest that it may have been used by [[berserker]]s to induce the rage state that they used in war.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Fatur|first=Karsten|date=2019-11-15|title=Sagas of the Solanaceae: Speculative ethnobotanical perspectives on the Norse berserkers |journal= [[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=244|article-number=112151|doi=10.1016/j.jep.2019.112151|pmid=31404578|s2cid=199548329 |issn=0378-8741|doi-access=}}</ref>

==Cultivation and use==
[[File:Henbane Hand book of pharmacy and therapeutics b1007511 004 tif c821gk83z.tiff|thumb|right|Henbane cultivation, Lilly Experimental Farm, 1919]]
Henbane originated in [[Eurasia]], and is now globally distributed<ref name="Roberts_31" /> as a plant grown mainly for pharmaceutical purposes. Henbane is rare in northern Europe; its cultivation for medicinal use is widespread and legal in central and eastern Europe and in India.<ref name=Raetsch05 /> Seeds of henbane from north-west Himalaya are reported to exhibit dormancy, and germination can be induced by the application of gibberellic acid, nitrates, sodium nitroprusside (SNP) and by moist cold stratification.<ref>Sharma S, Sharma RK (2010). Long-term storage-dependent changes in seed physiological aspects of ''Hyoscyamus niger'' from a cold desert region of Trans-Himalaya. International Journal of Plant Biology 1:e17: 84–88. https://doi.org/10.4081/pb.2010.e17</ref> Sharma (2024) observed that fully matured seeds of ''H. niger'' exhibited dormancy and in contrast, the comparatively immature seeds germinated well. The latter can be manipulated for the propagation of Henbane without seed pre-treatments.<ref>Sharma RK (2024). Harvesting seeds before dormancy induction in ''Hyoscyamus niger'', a threatened medicinal herb of trans Himalaya: implication for propagation without seed pre-treatments. Discov. Plants 1, 13 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1007/s44372-024-00013-2</ref> 

Henbane is used in traditional herbal medicine for ailments of the bones, rheumatism, toothache, asthma, cough, nervous diseases, and stomach pain. It might also be used as analgesic, sedative, and narcotic in some cultures.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Alizadeh A, Moshiri M, Alizadeh J, Balali-Mood M |title=Black henbane and its toxicity - a descriptive review |journal=Avicenna J Phytomed |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=297–311 |date=September 2014 |pmid=25386392 |pmc=4224707 }}</ref> Adhesive bandages with henbane extract behind the ear are reported to prevent discomfort in travel-sick people.{{medical citation needed|date=September 2018}} Henbane oil is used for medicinal massage.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |chapter=H. § Hyoscyamus|last=Lindequist|first=U. |publisher=Springer |year=1993 |editor-last=von Bruchhausen |editor-first=F. |display-editors=etal|title=Hagers Handbuch der pharmazeutischen Praxis |edition=5th |volume=5 |pages=460–474 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-57993-6_4 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-57993-6_4 |isbn=978-3-642-57993-6}}</ref>

Henbane material in most Western countries can be bought in pharmacies with a prescription only. Sales of henbane oil are not legally regulated and are allowed in shops other than pharmacies in the US.<ref name=Raetsch05 />

Henbane has travelled through the company of [[Romani people]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ODrIXj-48RsC&dq=gypsies+medicinal+herb&pg=PA147|title=Tibetan Medicinal Plants|page=147|isbn=978-0-8493-0031-8 |last1=Kletter |first1=Christa |last2=Kriechbaum |first2=Monika |date=2001 |publisher=CRC Press |oclc=1412543684}}</ref>

==Preparation, dosage, toxicity==
Henbane leaves and herbage without roots are chopped and dried and are then used for medicinal purposes or in incense and smoking blends, in making beer and tea, and in seasoning wine. Henbane leaves are boiled in oil to derive henbane oil. Henbane seeds are an ingredient in incense blends.<ref name=Raetsch05 />  In all preparations, the dosage has to be carefully estimated as henbane is highly toxic. For some therapeutic applications, dosages like 0.5 g and 1.5–3 g were used. The lethal dosage is not known.<ref name=":1" />

Henbane is toxic to cattle, wild animals, fish, and birds.<ref name=Raetsch05 /> Not all animals are susceptible; for example, the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera]] species, including [[cabbage moth]]s, eat henbane. Pigs are immune to henbane toxicity and are reported to enjoy the effects of the plant.<ref name=Raetsch05 />

== Psychoactive material ==

[[Hyoscyamine]], [[scopolamine]], and other [[tropane alkaloids]] have been found in the foliage and seeds of the plant.<ref name="Roberts_31" /> The standard alkaloid content has been reported to be 0.03% to 0.28%.<ref name=Raetsch05 />

The [[lignanamides]] [[hyoscyamide]], [[grossamide]], and [[cannabisins]] [[Cannabisin D|D]] and [[Cannabisin G|G]] have been identified in the seeds of Hyoscyamus niger.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Cui-Ying |last2=Liu |first2=Wing Keung |last3=Che |first3=Chun-Tao |title=Lignanamides and Nonalkaloidal Components of Hyoscyamus niger Seeds |url=https://pubs.acs.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-05-04 |journal=Journal of Natural Products |date=2002 |volume=65 |issue=2 |pages=206–209 |doi=10.1021/np010073b |pmid=11858758 |bibcode=2002JNAtP..65..206M |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Its psychoactive and pharmacological effects are a result of these alkaloids exerting an [[anticholinergic]] mechanism of action which blocks the function of [[acetylcholine]] in the brain and [[Receptor antagonism|antagonizes]] the [[muscarinic receptors]].<ref name="Kennedy 2014"/><ref name=Volgin18>{{cite journal | title=Understanding Central Nervous System Effects of Deliriant Hallucinogenic Drugs through Experimental Animal Models | journal= ACS Chemical Neuroscience | date=16 October 2018 | pmid= 30252437 | last1= Volgin | first1= A. D. | last2= Yakovlev | first2= O. A. | last3= Demin | first3= K. A. | last4= Alekseeva | first4= P. A. | last5= Kyzar | first5= E. J. | last6= Collins | first6= C. | last7= Nichols | first7= D. E. | last8= Kalueff | first8= A. V. | volume= 10 | issue= 1 | pages= 143–154 | doi= 10.1021/acschemneuro.8b00433 | s2cid= 52824516 }}</ref> This results in an altered state of consciousness, hallucinogenic experiences, and typically, [[delirium]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Duncan |first1=D. F. |last2=Gold |first2=R. S. |title=Drugs and the Whole Person |publisher=Wiley |date=1982 |isbn=0-471-04120-3 |oclc=7946443}}</ref><ref name="Kuklin">{{cite book | last = Kuklin | first = Alexander | title = How Do Witches Fly?| publisher = DNA Press |date=1999 | isbn = 0-9664027-0-7 |oclc=41923898}}</ref> This mechanism of action is not only linked to dangerous effects and accidents, but [[dementia]] as well.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lycaeum.org/mv/mu/datura.html |title=Datura Items |publisher=Lycaeum |access-date=2011-01-04 |archive-date=2010-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101003095140/http://www.lycaeum.org/mv/mu/datura.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.alzheimers.org.uk/site/scripts/news_article.php?newsID=2300 |title = Study suggests link between long-term use of anticholinergics and dementia risk |publisher = [[Alzheimer's Society]] |date = 26 January 2015 |access-date = 17 February 2015 |url-status = live |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151112115547/https://www.alzheimers.org.uk/site/scripts/news_article.php?newsID=2300 |archive-date = 12 November 2015 }}</ref><ref name=Volgin18/> Since toxicity/lethality is such a major concern with plants like henbane, many traditional preparations of henbane or other similar scopolamine-containing plants were designed to be applied [[Transdermal administration|transdermally]], often in "[[Flying ointment|magical ointments]]" by herbalists, witches and [[cunning folk]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Christian |last=Rätsch |title=The Encyclopedia of Psychoactive Plants: Ethnopharmacology and Its Applications |publisher=Park Street Press |date=2005 |isbn=978-1-59477-662-5 |oclc=883127124}}</ref><ref name= "Hansen">{{cite book |first=Harold A. |last=Hansen |title=The Witch's Garden |publisher=Unity Press |date=1978 |isbn=978-0-913300-47-3 |oclc=3770563}}  </ref><ref name="Fatur 140–158"/> The purpose of this was to absorb the primary and transdermally-active alkaloid scopolamine through the skin, thus eliminating the risk of the additional toxicity from [[atropine]] and hyoscyamine that is inevitably present with oral ingestion of the plant but not with topical use.<ref>{{cite book| last= Sollmann| first= Torald | title= A Manual of Pharmacology and Its Applications to Therapeutics and Toxicology | edition=8th| publisher= W. B. Saunders| place= Philadelphia and London | year= 1957}}</ref><ref name="Hansen"/>

==Effects==
Henbane ingestion by humans is followed simultaneously by peripheral inhibition and central stimulation.<ref name=Raetsch05 /> Common effects of henbane ingestion include hallucinations,<ref name="Roberts_31" /> dilated pupils, narcosis, restlessness, and flushed skin. Less common effects are [[tachycardia]], convulsions, vomiting, [[hypertension]], [[hyperpyrexia]], and [[ataxia]].<ref name="Roberts_31" /> Initial effects typically last for three to four hours, while aftereffects may last up to three days. The side effects of henbane ingestion are dryness in the mouth, confusion, visual illusions, bizarre thoughts, locomotor and memory disturbances, and farsightedness, similar in style to those of other tropane-based [[deliriants]], such as plants of the New World genus ''[[Datura]]''. As a result of this distinct chemical and pharmacological profile, overdoses can result not only in delirium, but also severe [[Toxidrome#Anticholinergic|anticholinergic syndrome]], coma, respiratory paralysis, and death. Low and average dosages have inebriating and aphrodisiac effects.<ref name=Raetsch05 /><ref name=":1" />

In his book ''How Do Witches Fly?'', Alexander Kuklin refers to an experience of black henbane had by German scientist Michael Schenck.<ref name="Kuklin"/> Schenck recalled his experience:

{{Blockquote|The henbane's first effect was purely physical discomfort. My limbs lost certainty, pains hammered in my head, and I began to feel extremely giddy ... I went to the mirror and was able to distinguish my face, but more dimly than normal. It looked flushed and must have been so. I had the feeling that my head had increased in size: it seemed to have grown broader, more solid, heavier, and I imagined that it was enveloped in firmer, thicker skin. The mirror itself seemed to be swaying, and I found it difficult to keep my face within its frame. The black discs of my pupils were immensely enlarged, as though the whole iris, which was normally blue, had become black. Despite of the dilation of my pupils I could see no better than usual; quite the contrary, the outlines of objects were hazy, the window and the window frame were obscured by a thin mist.}}

Schenck's pulse became rapid and he experienced a further increase in the hallucinogenic effects of the plant:

{{Blockquote|There were animals which looked at me keenly with contorted grimaces and staring, terrified eyes; there were terrifying stones and clouds of mist, all sweeping along in the same direction. They carried me irresistibly with them. Their coloring must be described—but it was not a pure hue. They enveloped in a vague gray light, which emitted a dull glow and rolled onward and upward into a black and smoky sky. I was flung into a flaring drunkenness, a witches' cauldron of madness. Above my head water was flowing, dark and blood-red. The sky was filled with herds of animals. Fluid, formless creatures emerged from the darkness. I heard words, but they were all wrong and nonsensical, and yet they possessed for me some hidden meaning.<ref name="Kuklin"/>}}

==Misidentification==
